content_units: This pattern—  upstairs external wall damp patches plus peeling paint near one window  —most often points to   rainwater ingress, failed window sealing, masonry defects, or local condensation around a cold bridge  , rather than rising damp. Because it is   non-urgent   and your first-phase budget is   £1,500  , the best approach is to   diagnose carefully before opening walls or paying for broad “damp treatment” packages  .
- Problem area:   upstairs external wall  , near   one window
- Likely UK house risks considered: exposed rain, ageing sealants, gutter overflow, cracked render/pointing, bridged cavities, and winter condensation
Likely Causes, Evidence to Gather, and Who Handles Them
Cause   Typical Clues   Evidence to Gather Before Calling   Best Specialist

Defective window sealant or failed window perimeter   Peeling paint concentrated at window reveal; staining after wind-driven rain; soft plaster near frame   Close-up photos of frame edges inside/outside; note whether patches worsen after rain; check gaps/cracked mastic   Window repair specialist or good general builder

Gutter, downpipe, hopper, or roof edge leak above wall   Damp patch appears after rain; staining tracks downward; issue higher up than window   Photos during/after rain if safe; look for overflow marks, loose joints, blocked gutters, wet masonry outside   Roofer or guttering contractor

Cracked render, failed pointing, porous brickwork, or masonry defect   External cracks, blown render, open joints, localized patch matching outside defect   Exterior photos from ground/binocular zoom; mark crack locations; compare inside patch to outside facade position   Bricklayer, facade repair contractor, or general builder

Cavity wall issue or bridged cavity near opening   Damp around window head/jamb; recurring despite repainting; worsens in heavy rain   Note exact damp shape around reveal; any prior insulation/window works; ask if cavity trays/weeps are present   Building surveyor first, then builder/bricklayer

Condensation from cold bridge/poor ventilation   Worse in cold weather; mould specks; mornings worse; behind curtains/blinds; not clearly rain-linked   Humidity readings, room temperature, window use, extractor use, photos of any black mould/condensation   Damp surveyor with building pathology focus or ventilation specialist

Plumbing leak less likely but possible   Patch persists in dry weather; unrelated to rainfall; nearby radiator/pipe route   Note whether area changes when heating is on; any pressure drop; pipe route sketch if known   Plumber
1) Build a simple evidence pack first
Spend   1-2 weeks   gathering enough detail to avoid guesswork.
- Take   dated photos   every 2-3 days and after heavy rain.
- Mark the damp patch edges lightly with painter’s tape or pencil on masking tape to see if it spreads.
- Photograph the   outside wall elevation  , especially:
- window head, sill, and side seals
- If possible, use a cheap hygrometer to log:
These are the best-value first moves within your budget.
- Check for   overflowing or blocked gutters   during rain.
- Inspect for   cracked or missing external sealant   around the window.
- Look for   hairline cracks   in render or failed pointing above the patch.
- Pull furniture slightly away from the wall and see if airflow is poor.
- Check whether condensation forms on or near that window in colder weather.
3) First professional visit should usually be diagnosis-led
For your symptoms, the most sensible first paid step is usually:
-   Independent building surveyor or damp/building pathology specialist
- Or, if exterior defects are obvious, a   roofer/general builder   for targeted external inspection
Avoid starting with a contractor whose only solution is a chemical damp-proof treatment unless a genuine diagnosis supports it.
4) Remedy external water-entry issues before internal redecoration
If there is any chance of rain penetration:
- then allow wall to dry before redecorating
- use appropriate stain block/breathable paint if advised
- redecorate only after moisture source is resolved
- Typical aim: identify whether this is   rain ingress vs condensation vs hidden defect
- Window resealing, minor pointing/render patch, gutter joint fix/clearance
- Hygrometer, photos, moisture revisit if needed
4.   Small internal making-good only if source is fixed
In many Bristol cases,   phase one can cover diagnosis plus one or two minor external repairs   such as:
Option 1:   Independent building surveyor     Best if cause is unclear and you want an unbiased diagnosis before works   Strongest first step for recurring damp
Option 2:   Roofer / guttering contractor     Best if patch worsens after rain and there is anything suspect above the window   High-value first repair path
Option 3:   Window repair specialist / builder     Best if paint failure clusters tightly around frame, sill, or reveal   Usually affordable first-phase fix
Option 4:   Bricklayer or facade repair contractor     Best if there are visible cracks, failed pointing, or damaged render outside   Good for rain penetration through masonry
